title: UN expert warns of new threats to Rohingya before ICJ ruling
excerpt: Kelley E Currie, UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar, ended an eight-day visit in Dhaka, urging sanctions and full use of the world court judgment.

image.alt: Shops and shelters along a lane in a Rohingya refugee camp, Cox's Bazar
image.credit: CAPTAIN RAJU / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
The UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, Kelley E Currie, said on Wednesday (18 November) she is "deeply concerned" about Myanmar's government and ultra-nationalist groups such as Ma Ba Tha, and warned of renewed violence against the Rohingya, bdnews24.com reported. She spoke at UN House in Dhaka on the last day of an eight-day visit.

The International Court of Justice is due to rule in The Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar on Thursday at 3pm Bangladesh time. Currie called the ruling a "pivotal moment" and said the evidence heard in the trial will stand whatever the verdict.

She described Myanmar's junta as "gangsters", The Daily Star reported, and said China and Russia shield Myanmar at the UN Security Council and supply it with arms. In remarks reported by The Daily Star, she also urged sanctions, said the Security Council could consider an arms embargo or a referral to the International Criminal Court, called for the judgment to be carried out in full, and asked for support for Bangladesh and other countries hosting refugees.

Currie also said donor cuts to protection, education, livelihoods and non-emergency health services are making the camps less safe, The Business Standard reported, citing UNB. She linked the cuts to drugs, trafficking, recruitment by armed groups and online gambling, and said gender-based violence and crimes against children are rising.

In the camps, refugees plan to watch the verdict on a big screen in Jamtholi, The Daily Star reported. Mohammad Mizanur Rahman, Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner, said: "Repatriation will not happen immediately as a direct consequence of the judgment."

Why it matters

The ruling will not change conditions in Cox's Bazar overnight, and agencies are already working with less money. Warnings of new violence in Rakhine point to a risk of more arrivals and more pressure on services in the camps.

What to watch

The ICJ judgment on 19 November, how Myanmar and the Security Council respond, and any sign of new movement across the border.
